title: Whose is it?
intro: This unit adds the last case ending, the genitive `-(n)Yň`, which says **of** or **'s**: *Aýna* → *Aýnanyň* (Aýna's). Together with the possessive endings of [A1 unit 9](a1-u09) it builds **Aýna's house**, *Aýnanyň öýi*, with an ending on each word. You also meet the small *n* that comes before a case ending after **his** or **her** (*öýünde*, in his house), and the question **whose?**, *kimiň?*

blocks.text: English says **Aýna's** or **of the house**. Turkmen uses an ending, the genitive (*eýelik düşüm*): after a consonant it is *-yň* or *-iň*, after a vowel *-nyň* or *-niň*. It follows vowel harmony like every ending, and it goes straight onto names, with no apostrophe: *Merdanyň*, *Aýnanyň*.

blocks.caption: Nouns and names in the genitive
head: Word
+ genitive
Meaning

blocks.text: The sound changes you know from [A1 unit 8](a1-u08) and [A1 unit 9](a1-u09) all apply, because the ending starts with a vowel after a consonant. *k*, *p* and *ç* soften (*kitabyň*, *çöregiň*), and so does the *t* of *Aşgabat* and *sagat* (watch, clock): *Aşgabadyň*, *sagadyň*. *ogul* drops its vowel: *ogluň*. And a final *e* becomes *ä* before *-niň*: *eje* → *ejäniň*, *gije* → *gijäniň*. Some writers keep the *e* (*ejeniň*); this course writes *ejäniň* and accepts both.
The personal pronouns have genitives too. You met *meniň* and *seniň* in [A1 unit 9](a1-u09); here is the whole set. Note the *n* in *onuň*, from *ol*.

blocks.title: Your book, or of the book?
blocks.text: After a consonant, the genitive looks just like **your** from [A1 unit 9](a1-u09): *kitabyň* is **your book** on its own, and **of the book** when a noun with the ending of **its** follows: *kitabyň ady*, the title of the book. After a vowel the two differ: *kakaň* (your father), *kakanyň* (the father's).

sections.title: Aýna's house: an ending on each word

blocks.text: To say **Aýna's house** or **the door of the house**, Turkmen puts an ending on both words. The owner comes first, in the genitive; the thing owned comes second, with the ending of **his** or **her** from [A1 unit 9](a1-u09), `-(s)Y`. *Aýnanyň öýi* is, word for word, **Aýna's her-house**.

lines: öýüň gapysy     the door of the house

blocks.text: The last line shows that an owner can already have an ending of its own: *kakam* (my father) + *-yň* = *kakamyň*, **my father's**.

**With the pronouns**, the thing owned takes the matching person: **my** with *meniň*, **your** with *seniň*, and so on. Because the ending already says whose it is, the pronoun is often left out: *kitabym* alone means **my book**. Keep it to stress or contrast: *Bu meniň kitabym, seniň kitabyň däl* (This is my book, not yours).

items.en: The door of the house is blue.

blocks.title: Two endings, not one
blocks.text: *Aýna öýi* and *Aýnanyň öý* are both wrong: the owner needs *-(n)Yň* and the thing owned needs *-(s)Y*, *Aýnanyň öýi*. With a pronoun, match the person: *meniň öýüm*, not *meniň öýi*.

blocks.title: Leaving out onuň
blocks.text: *Kakasy mugallym* already means **his (or her) father is a teacher**. Add *onuň* when it helps: *Merdan we Batyr dost. Onuň kakasy mugallym* says it is one boy's father.

sections.title: öýünde: the n after his and her

blocks.text: When a case ending follows the ending of **his, her, its** or **their**, a small *n* comes in between: *öýi* (his house) → *öýünde* (in his house), *kakasy* (her father) → *kakasyna* (to her father). Grammars call it the pronominal *n*. It comes **only** after that ending: with **my**, **your**, **our** the case ending goes straight on, *öýümde*, *öýüňde*, *öýümizde*.

Two details in the table. After the *n*, the object ending is just *-y* or *-i*: *kakasyny*, *öýüni*. And the *i* of *öýi* rounds to *ü* once something follows it, by the rounding rule of [A1 unit 3](a1-u03): *öýi*, but *öýünde*, *öýüne*.

In **Aýna's house** the case ending goes on the second word, with its *n*: *Aýnanyň öýünde* (at Aýna's house), *Merdanyň kakasyna* (to Merdan's father), *mekdebiň gapysyndan* (from the school's door).

items.en: The book is in Merdan's bag.
We are going to Aýna's house.
The guests are at the school door.

blocks.title: Don't forget the n
blocks.text: *Aýnanyň öýde* and *sumkasyda* are wrong: after **his** or **her** comes the *n*, *Aýnanyň öýünde*, *sumkasynda*. And don't add it after **my** or **your**: *öýümde*, not *öýümnde*.

sections.title: Whose? kimiň? and who has it? kimde?

blocks.text: *kim* (who) takes the genitive like any noun: *kimiň*, **whose**. The thing owned takes the ending of **his** or **her**, as after any owner: *Bu kimiň kitaby?*, Whose book is this? The answer puts the owner in the same place: *Bu Aýnanyň kitaby*, *Bu meniň kitabym*.

To ask **who has it** (on them, right now), use the locative of *kim*: *kimde?*, as in *mende* and *sende* from [A1 unit 5](a1-u05). *Açar kimde? — Açar Merjende.* (Who has the key? — Merjen has the key.)

items.tk: Bu kimiň öýi? — Bu biziň öýümiz.
items.seg: Bu kim|iň öý|i? — Bu biz|iň öý|ümiz.
items.en: Whose house is this? — It's our house.
Whose house are we going to?
Who has the key? — I do.
Who has the money? — My father does.

blocks.title: Ine!
blocks.text: To hand something over, say *ine*, **here it is**: *Ine, kitabyň!* Here's your book!

summary: The genitive `-(n)Yň` says **of** or **'s**: *-yň, -iň* (rounded *-uň, -üň*) after a consonant, *-nyň, -niň* after a vowel: *Merdanyň*, *öýüň*, *Aýnanyň*. No apostrophe on names.
Pronouns: *meniň, seniň, onuň, biziň, siziň, olaryň*.
**Aýna's house** has an ending on each word: *Aýnanyň öýi*, *öýüň gapysy*. With a pronoun, match the person: *meniň öýüm*; the pronoun can be dropped.
After **his, her, its, their**, a case ending takes an *n* first: *öýünde, kakasyna, adyny*. Not after **my** or **your**: *öýümde*.
**Whose?** is *kimiň?*: *Bu kimiň kitaby?* **Who has it?** is *kimde?*
